summary: This informational document provides a framework for Layer 2 Provider Provisioned Virtual Private Networks. It is meant to help standardize protocols and mechanisms so that different L2VPN implementations can interoperate.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC maps out how a provider can offer Layer 2 connectivity over a shared network. It explains the service models and the components that connect customer devices through provider equipment.

questions: what is a provider edge router
what is the difference between vpws and vpls
subtitle: The models and functional components used to describe provider-run Layer 2 VPNs.

tldr.problem: Providers need interoperable ways to connect customer Layer 2 networks across a shared packet-switched backbone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes VPWS, VPLS, and IPLS models and the shared components used to transport frames, including attachment circuits, pseudowires, forwarders, tunnels, and signaling.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework that compares approaches and issues but does not select a particular design.

today: RFC 4664 is an Informational framework published in September 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Layer 2 VPN Services
sections.content:
The framework covers VPNs that a service provider helps manage and provision. It describes reference models and technical issues that matter to interoperable solutions, including security, but it does not choose a particular technical approach.

It distinguishes a Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS), which provides point-to-point Layer 2 connectivity, from a Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS), which emulates a LAN across a wide-area network. It also describes an IP-only LAN-like service for IP hosts and routers.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider can connect two customer locations with a virtual point-to-point link or make several locations appear to share a LAN. This framework explains both service models and a related IP-only option.

sections.title: Reference Models and Components
sections.content:
In a VPWS, customer-edge devices connect to provider-edge devices through attachment circuits. A pseudowire carries frames between provider edges through a tunnel in the provider network. Each VPWS forwarder maps one attachment circuit to one pseudowire.

In VPLS, provider-edge bridge modules connect to an emulated LAN made from VPLS forwarders and pseudowires. A forwarder can map multiple attachment circuits to multiple pseudowires. The framework also allows provider-edge functions to be split between a user-facing PE and a network-facing PE.
sections.plainLanguage: An attachment circuit links a customer to the provider. Pseudowires carry frames between provider-edge devices, where forwarding functions connect the customer links to those pseudowires.

sections.title: Transport, Forwarding, and Signaling
sections.content:
A pseudowire carries frames between two provider-edge devices; a tunnel can carry one or more pseudowires. Each receiving PE must be able to identify which pseudowire carried a frame. The forwarder selects the outgoing pseudowire or attachment circuit using the incoming connection and, depending on the service, frame contents or forwarding information.

Pseudowire signaling distributes identifiers, selects the remote forwarder, communicates relevant state changes, and establishes shared characteristics. If the attachment circuits use different technologies, the endpoints need an agreed method for interworking and compatible maximum transmission units.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel is the path between provider edges, and the pseudowire identifies a service carried on that path. Signaling gives both ends the information they need to connect the right customer links.

sections.title: How VPWS, VPLS, and IPLS Forward
sections.content:
VPWS forwards frames according to the virtual circuit, not the frame’s Layer 2 contents. VPLS forwarders learn source MAC addresses from pseudowires and use them to send known unicast frames to a selected destination. Frames with unknown or multicast destinations are sent to other forwarders in the emulated LAN.

VPLS overlay topologies need rules that prevent forwarding loops. A full mesh requires each virtual switch instance to avoid forwarding a frame received over one pseudowire onto another. The framework notes that a full mesh requires n*(n-1) pseudowires between participating VPLS PEs, which can create scaling problems. IPLS can reduce the need for MAC learning by carrying only IP traffic and using control-plane information.
sections.plainLanguage: VPWS sends traffic along a fixed virtual circuit. VPLS uses MAC addresses to choose a destination and floods frames when it does not know the destination; the overlay needs rules to prevent loops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Provider-edge devices should not accept control connections from arbitrary peers. Providers can configure known peers or rely on trusted discovery. For connections between providers, the RFC recommends cryptographic authentication, and it notes that processing-rate limits can reduce denial-of-service effects.

The framework also describes attacks on VPLS forwarding, including many unknown or multicast destinations and false source MAC addresses that fill address tables. L2VPN procedures do not provide authentication, integrity, or privacy for customer traffic; customers must provide those protections when they need them.
sections.plainLanguage: Provider devices need to verify their control peers and limit excessive control traffic. The VPN framework does not make customer traffic private or protect it from tampering.
